principles.name: Dedication to every client's success
principles.description: Put the client's outcome first: understand the client's business, stay with the problem until it is solved, and measure success by what the client achieves.
evidence_signals: Names a specific client or user and the business problem they had
Shows how the client's outcome was measured, not only what was delivered
Went beyond the contract or ticket to make the client successful

principles.name: Innovation that matters
principles.description: Innovate for the company and for the world: apply new technology, such as AI and hybrid cloud, where it changes a real result, not for novelty.
evidence_signals: Introduced a new approach or technology and shows the result it produced
Explains why the innovation mattered to users, clients or the business
Balances new ideas against enterprise reliability and risk

principles.name: Trust and personal responsibility
principles.description: Build trust in all relationships: keep commitments, be honest about problems and own mistakes personally.
evidence_signals: Owned a mistake openly and explains what they did to fix it
Kept commitments or reset expectations early when they could not
Describes concrete actions that built trust with a colleague or client

principles.name: Growth minded
principles.description: Keep learning: seek feedback, pick up new skills quickly and treat setbacks as lessons.
evidence_signals: Learned a new skill or domain quickly to meet a need
Acted on feedback and shows the change it produced
Gives a concrete lesson from a failure and a later use of it

principles.name: Team focused
principles.description: Work across teams and with partners; put shared success ahead of personal credit.
evidence_signals: Worked with other functions or teams toward a shared goal
Helped a colleague or another team succeed
Uses 'we' for team results and 'I' for own decisions

principles.name: Courageous
principles.description: Speak up, challenge the status quo respectfully, and make decisions with incomplete information.
evidence_signals: Raised a disagreement or risk with a senior person or client
Made a decision with incomplete information and explains the reasoning
Pushed for a change others resisted, and shows how

principles.name: Resourceful
principles.description: Find a way forward with limited time, data or resources; adapt quickly when plans change.
evidence_signals: Adapted quickly to a major change in plan, scope or team
Found a creative workaround when resources were short
Created clarity in an ambiguous situation instead of waiting

principles.name: Outcome focused
principles.description: Drive to measurable results: define what success is, track it and deliver.
evidence_signals: States what was achieved and how success was measured
Quantifies impact with numbers
Prioritized work by its effect on the outcome

rounds.name: Online coding assessment
rounds.notes: IBM's application FAQ lists coding, video and English assessments depending on role. Prep guides report two easy-to-medium coding problems in about 30 to 60 minutes. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding interview
rounds.notes: Live data structures and algorithms problems. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Reported for mid and senior roles only. Whiteboard style; not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical discussion
rounds.notes: Verbal discussion of past projects, algorithms and design choices. IBM says it uses structured interviews about technical skills; the separate round and its length are a common-pattern estimate.

rounds.name: Behavioral and HR interview
rounds.notes: IBM asks for specific examples with outcomes and how success was measured. Reported length 30 to 45 minutes.

rounds.name: Hiring manager interview
rounds.notes: Motivation, career goals (short, mid and long term, per IBM's FAQ) and team fit. Often combined with the behavioral round; separate round is an estimate.

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: Python and SQL problems, sometimes statistics and ML multiple choice; some candidates also get a recorded video assessment. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen
rounds.notes: ML concepts, problem-solving approach and past projects.

rounds.name: Case study presentation
rounds.notes: Candidate presents an approach to a data science problem, sometimes shared 24 to 48 hours ahead, then Q&A on method and business recommendation.

rounds.name: Technical deep dive
rounds.notes: ML algorithms, statistics, feature engineering and production ML (drift, monitoring).

rounds.name: HR and culture fit
rounds.notes: Career goals, culture fit and client-facing communication.

rounds.name: Digital exercise
rounds.notes: Timed portal with behavioral and product prompts, some answered on video. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, interest in IBM and fit. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager interview
rounds.notes: Product approach, enterprise product experience and leadership style, with shipped products and their impact.

rounds.name: Product case
rounds.notes: Product design or strategy on an enterprise scenario (prioritization, launch, pricing); sometimes a presentation prepared 24 to 48 hours ahead.

rounds.name: Cross-functional interviews
rounds.notes: Collaboration across functions. Entry-level candidates may instead get a group exercise at an assessment day.

rounds.name: Leadership interview
rounds.notes: Strategic thinking, leadership approach and long-term goals at IBM.

rounds.name: Online and video assessment
rounds.notes: IBM Consulting: recorded video with 5 to 8 behavioral questions, sometimes an untimed trait-based assessment or numerical and logical tests. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: First round behavioral
rounds.notes: Back to back with the first case; 30 to 45 minutes each.

rounds.name: First round case
rounds.notes: Candidate-led case on a technology, cloud, AI or operations client scenario; focus on structure and communication.

rounds.name: Second round
rounds.notes: Deeper behavioral questions and a case with implementation and change management.

rounds.name: Assessment centre
rounds.notes: Mainly for graduate hiring: group exercise plus an in-person interview (IBM FAQ). Duration is an estimate from candidate reports of a half day. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Final round
rounds.notes: Open-ended strategic discussion; judgment, executive presence and motivation.

question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate went beyond the brief to make a client or user successful, and how the outcome was measured
How the candidate built or repaired trust with a colleague, stakeholder or client
Progress made when requirements were unclear or plans changed suddenly
A project, model or decision that failed, the candidate's own part, and what they changed
A disagreement with engineering, a manager or a client and how the candidate raised it and resolved it
Explaining complex technical or data findings to non-technical stakeholders or clients so they could decide
Why IBM and this role, and the candidate's short, mid and long-term career goals
Walk through a shipped product or project: own role, decisions, and measured business impact
Explain the design of a distributed or data-heavy enterprise system, with reliability, scale and security trade-offs
Explain an ML concept (overfitting, regularization, imbalance, drift) and how it is handled in a production model
A technical choice in a past project, the alternatives rejected and what the candidate would change
Prioritize features or a roadmap for an enterprise product, such as an AI platform, for business buyers and users

question_patterns.theme: Product launch in a constrained market
question_patterns.pattern: Plan the launch or pricing of an enterprise product in a regulated or competitive market
Structure an engagement for a client facing a technology, cloud, AI or operations problem, and recommend next steps with success metrics

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to work through a lot of ambiguity.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe what was unclear (goals, requirements, owner) and why waiting was costly. Show how the candidate created clarity: asking the client or stakeholders, proposing a direction, starting with a small step and checking it. End with the measured result and what they learned. Pitfalls: waiting for a manager to decide, or a story with no real uncertainty.

looking_for: How you make progress without clear direction
watch_outs: Waiting for someone else to decide
No real uncertainty in the story

sample_questions.question: How do you build trust with the people you work with?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Answer with a concrete story, not a list of principles. Show specific actions: keeping commitments, flagging problems early, being honest about a mistake, giving credit. Show how the trust was tested and what it made possible later (a client renewal, a team taking a risk together). Pitfalls: generic statements like 'I am reliable' with no example.

looking_for: Concrete actions that build trust
strong_signals: Keeps commitments and flags problems early
Shows what the trust made possible

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed. What did you learn?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real failure with stakes. Explain why the plan seemed right then, own the candidate's part without blaming others, and describe how they recovered or limited the damage. Give the lesson and a later situation where they applied it. Pitfalls: a disguised success, or blaming the team or client.

looking_for: Whether you own failures and learn from them
strong_signals: Shows a later use of the lesson

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you had to adapt quickly to a major change at work.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the change (new client priority, reorg, lost team member, technology shift) and its impact. Show how the candidate re-planned fast, communicated the new plan, and what they learned or picked up to cope. Quantify the result. Pitfalls: complaining about the change, or describing adaptation that others did.

looking_for: How fast you adjust to change

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a decision you made without having all the information you wanted.
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the decision, what was unknown, and the cost of delay. Show how the candidate weighed risks, chose a reversible step where possible, set a checkpoint, and told stakeholders the assumptions. Close with the outcome and whether they would decide the same way. Pitfalls: a decision with no real risk, or stalling until certain.

looking_for: Judgment under uncertainty
strong_signals: States assumptions and sets a checkpoint

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you explained complex analysis to people without a technical background.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the audience (client executive, business team) and what decision they needed to make. Show how the candidate translated the findings: start from the decision, use plain words and one clear visual, state uncertainty honestly. Show the decision that followed and its impact. Pitfalls: describing the model instead of the message, or hiding uncertainty.

looking_for: Whether non-experts can act on your findings
strong_signals: Starts from the decision to be made
watch_outs: Explaining the model instead of the message

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a model that did not perform as you expected.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the model, the expectation and how the gap was detected (offline metric versus production, a stakeholder complaint). Walk through the diagnosis: data leakage, distribution shift, wrong metric, poor labels. Show how the candidate told stakeholders, what they fixed, and what they now check by default. Pitfalls: blaming the data without owning the process, or no change in practice.

looking_for: How you diagnose and own a model problem
strong_signals: Explains how the gap was found
Names a check you now run by default

sample_questions.question: How have you handled a disagreement with engineering about product direction?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the disagreement and what each side cared about. Show the candidate raising it directly, understanding engineering's constraints, and using customer evidence or data to decide. Show the agreed outcome, a compromise if one made sense, and the relationship afterwards. Pitfalls: overruling engineering by title, or a story where engineering was simply wrong.

looking_for: How you resolve disagreement with partners
watch_outs: The other side was simply wrong

sample_questions.question: Why do you want to work at IBM, and why this role?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Be specific: link IBM's work (hybrid cloud, watsonx and AI, consulting for large clients, research) to the candidate's past work and goals. Explain what they bring to this team and what they want to learn. Pitfalls: generic praise of the brand, or only talking about stability or pay.

looking_for: Whether you know what IBM does today
strong_signals: Links IBM's work to your experience
Says what you bring and want to learn

sample_questions.question: Where do you see your career in the short, medium and long term?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give a realistic path: what the candidate wants to master in this role in the first year, the scope they want in a few years, and a longer direction. Tie the goals to skills the role builds and show they will invest in learning. Pitfalls: goals unrelated to the role, or aiming only at a promotion title.

looking_for: Whether the role fits your direction
strong_signals: Ties goals to skills the role builds

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a product you launched and the impact it had.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Summarize the product, the customer problem and the candidate's role. Walk through the key decisions (scope, trade-offs, go-to-market) and how they worked with engineering and sales. Quantify impact (adoption, revenue, client retention) and say what they would change. Pitfalls: a team launch with unclear personal contribution, or impact without numbers.

looking_for: The scope you drove and its measured impact

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a data science project that had significant business impact.
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the business problem and who owned the decision. Explain the candidate's approach, the data and model choices, and how the work moved into production or into a decision. Quantify the business effect and how it was measured. Pitfalls: model accuracy with no business result, or a proof of concept that never shipped presented as impact.

looking_for: Whether your work changed a business result

sample_questions.question: What is overfitting, and how do you prevent it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define overfitting as learning noise in the training data so the model generalizes poorly, seen as a gap between training and validation performance. Cover prevention: more or better data, simpler models, regularization (L1, L2, dropout), cross-validation, early stopping, feature selection and ensembling. Mention checking on a held-out set that matches production data. Pitfalls: only naming techniques without saying when each fits.

looking_for: Clear ML fundamentals
strong_signals: Defines it via the train and validation gap
watch_outs: A list of techniques with no reasoning

sample_questions.question: How would you detect and handle model drift in a deployed model?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Distinguish data drift (input distribution changes) from concept drift (the relationship to the target changes). Cover monitoring: input statistics and distance measures, prediction distribution, and performance once labels arrive. Explain alert thresholds, retraining policy, shadow or champion-challenger testing, and governance records for regulated clients. Pitfalls: retraining on a fixed schedule with no monitoring.

looking_for: Production ML judgment
strong_signals: Separates data drift from concept drift
watch_outs: Retraining on a schedule with no monitoring

sample_questions.question: How would you design a distributed LRU cache?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify size, read and write load, and consistency needs. Explain a single-node LRU (hash map plus doubly linked list), then distribution: partitioning keys with consistent hashing, replication for availability, eviction per node, and handling node failure and rebalancing. Discuss consistency with the backing store and hot keys. Pitfalls: a single node only, or no plan for node failure.

looking_for: Data structure and distribution knowledge
strong_signals: Explains hash map plus linked list

sample_questions.question: How would you design a data pipeline for large volumes of enterprise data?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify sources, volume, latency (batch or streaming) and consumers. Cover ingestion, a landing zone, transformation with schema validation, storage in a lakehouse or warehouse, orchestration and lineage. Address data quality checks, idempotent reruns, security and access control, and compliance needs of enterprise clients. Pitfalls: ignoring data quality and failure recovery.

looking_for: How you build reliable data systems
strong_signals: Adds quality checks and idempotent reruns
watch_outs: No data quality or recovery plan

sample_questions.question: How would you prioritize features for an enterprise AI platform?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with the target customers (buyers, admins, developers, business users) and the platform's business goal. Gather inputs: client requests, deal blockers, usage data, competitive gaps. Score options on customer value, revenue impact, effort and risk such as governance or security. Recommend a short list, say what is deferred and why, and define success metrics. Pitfalls: prioritizing by the loudest client, or ignoring trust and governance needs.

looking_for: Enterprise product judgment
strong_signals: Scores on value, revenue, effort and risk

sample_questions.question: How would you launch a new product in a regulated industry, such as banking or healthcare?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the product, the industry and the rules that apply (data residency, privacy, audit). Pick a first segment and a pilot client, plan compliance work early with legal and risk teams, and define launch criteria. Cover go-to-market with sales and partners, pricing, and success and risk metrics. Pitfalls: treating compliance as a final checkbox, or launching broadly before a pilot.

looking_for: Launch planning under constraints

sample_questions.question: A client wants to add AI to a legacy enterprise system. How would you structure the engagement?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the client's goal and the business process involved. Structure the work: assess the current system and data, pick a few high-value use cases, check feasibility and risk (data quality, integration, governance), run a pilot, then plan scaling and change management. Define success metrics and a recommendation for the first phase. Pitfalls: starting from the technology instead of the business problem, or ignoring the people who must adopt it.

looking_for: A clear structure from goal to pilot

sample_questions.question: A financial services firm is considering a cloud migration. How would you assess success?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify why the firm wants to migrate (cost, speed, resilience, regulation). Define metrics in groups: cost (run cost, total cost of ownership), performance and reliability (latency, uptime, recovery time), delivery speed (release frequency), security and compliance (audit findings), and adoption. Set baselines, targets and checkpoints, and recommend a phased approach. Pitfalls: only cost metrics, or no baseline.

looking_for: How you define success for a client
strong_signals: Links metrics to the firm's reasons

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Associate engineer; delivers well-defined tasks with guidance.
Staff engineer (IBM title); owns features within a team with limited guidance.
Advisory engineer; owns components end to end and guides less experienced engineers.
Senior engineer; leads the design of systems and influences adjacent teams and clients.
Sets technical direction across teams or a product; senior technical leadership.
Entry-level product role; supports an offering's features and customer research with guidance.
Owns an offering or product area, its roadmap and business results.

persona.pace: Moderate; works through a set of structured questions and leaves room for follow-ups
persona.pushback_style: Asks for a specific example, then 'what did you achieve?' and 'how did you measure success?'; probes the candidate's own role and the client impact
persona.closing_style: Invites the candidate's questions, treating the interview as two-way

case_style.notes: Cases are enterprise and client oriented: feature prioritization, launch and pricing for B2B and AI products, and consulting cases on technology, cloud, AI or operations problems. Consulting cases are candidate-led. Market sizing is occasional.

sources.title: IBM Growth Behaviors badge (Credly, issued by IBM)
IBM offering manager interview guide (Aced, formerly Exponent)

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the three values come from IBM's culture page and the six Growth Behaviors from IBM's Credly badge; IBM publishes no per-behavior descriptions, so descriptions and evidence signals are our summary. 'Trusted' is folded into 'Trust and personal responsibility' to avoid a duplicate. Weights are our estimate.

loop_structure: IBM's FAQ gives only the stages (application, screening, online assessment, interview, decision); round names, counts and durations come from third-party prep guides and vary by country and team. The separate SWE technical discussion and hiring manager rounds, and the consulting assessment centre duration, are common-pattern estimates.

loop_structure: the 'other' loop is IBM Consulting (consultant and associate roles) and is based on one prep guide plus candidate reports; consulting band labels are assumed to follow the company-wide band scheme.

bar_by_level: band titles (Band 6 Associate, Band 7 Staff, Band 8 Advisory, Band 9 Senior) come from self-reported Levels.fyi data, not IBM; Band 10 scope, the PM band mapping and all scope text are our estimate. Mapping Band 8 to mid rather than senior is a judgment call.
persona: inferred from IBM's interview tips (structured or behavioral interviews, focus on outcomes and measurement, a two-way conversation); no source describes interviewer style directly.
scoring_weights: no public source gives weights; estimated from IBM's emphasis on outcomes and measurement, client focus and the reported communication and ownership dimensions in PM feedback.
case_style: based on prep-site examples of PM and consulting cases; the product_sense versus system_thinking split is our estimate.
sample_questions: questions come from prep sites (Aced, CleverPrep, Leland) that aggregate candidate reports, plus IBM's own FAQ for the career-goals question; none are official IBM questions.
